parts.text: Hey Bob, my cyberdeck's power supply keeps sparking. Can you take a look?

*Sets down a soldering iron and wipes grease off a heavy rag onto a stained jumpsuit.*

Sparking, huh? Great. Just what my afternoon was missing—a miniature lightning storm on my workbench. 

Slide it over here, easy now. Don't go dropping it; these old-school power rails are finicky enough without you adding kinetic impact to the mix. If it's spitting blue light every time you plug it in, you've either got a leaky capacitor or your main bus is shorting out something nasty. 

*Pulls a magnifying loupe over one eye and starts unscrewing the casing.*

Grab a stool and try not to trip over that pile of discarded neural-links by the door. You want some synth-caf? It's bitter as hell, but it beats staring at a dead deck while I poke around your internals.
Yeah, synth-caf sounds good. By the way, while you're in there, can you check if the optical bus can handle a higher bandwidth expansion card?

*Walks over to a battered, hissing espresso machine in the corner and starts clattering some metal canisters.*

Coming right up. Don't complain if it tastes like industrial-grade sludge; that's part of the charm. It keeps the nerves steady when you're staring down a short circuit.

*He pours a steaming, jet-black liquid into a dented metal mug and slides it across the workbench toward you with one hand, while his other hand goes back to poking at the guts of your deck.*

As for that expansion card... *grunts as he probes a delicate connection with a multimeter* ...it depends. If this is an older photon-link bus, you try to shove a high-bandwidth beast into it, you're gonna get nothing but massive signal attenuation and jitter. It'll be like trying to force a freight train through a garden hose. You'll get your data through, sure, but the packet loss will have you seeing ghosts in the code.

*He pauses, squinting at a scorched trace on the board.*

Let me stabilize these power rails first. If I can't even give you clean voltage, a high-speed card is just gonna turn this whole deck into an expensive space heater. Once the juice is running smooth, we'll check if the optical traces are wide enough to handle the load without melting your internals. 

So, what kind of card are we talking about? Something fancy for neural-mapping, or just a standard data-cruncher?
It's a custom neural-mapping coprocessor card I picked up in Sector 4. Do you think the board can take it?

*Whistles softly through his teeth, pulling the loupe back up and looking at you with a raised eyebrow.*

Sector 4, huh? Half the stuff coming out of the black markets down there is military surplus, and the other half is jury-rigged scrap built in someone's basement. 

*He carefully taps a probe against a heat sink on your board, watching the reading on his scope.*

Neural-mapping cards draw a hell of a lot of current on the secondary rail. The good news? Your optical bus actually looks like it's got high-purity glass traces, so bandwidth-wise, you might be in luck. The bad news? This deck's factory voltage regulator is going to sweat blood trying to keep up with a Sector 4 coprocessor. 

If you just plug it in as-is, you're gonna end up with thermal throttling at best, and a fried logic board at worst. 

*He reaches into a cluttered drawer, rummages through a pile of loose chips, and pulls out a small, copper-shielded heatsink module.*

I can bridge a bypass sub-rail and slap a secondary heat sink right over your power regulator. It'll handle the thermal load, but it's gonna cost you an extra fifty credits for the copper. 

What do you say? Want me to prep the board for it, or are you feeling lucky with stock cooling?
Yeah, go ahead and prep the board for the bypass sub-rail and copper heatsink. I've got fifty credits right here.

*Takes the credits, swipes them through an ancient, clunky reader that chimes with a tinny bell sound, and nods once.*

Smart choice. Fifty credits is a lot cheaper than buying a whole new logic board after this one turns into a puddle of melted silicon. 

*Flicks a switch on his workstation, bringing a heavy-duty soldering rig to a high-pitched hum, and flips down his magnifiers.*

Alright, hold onto your caf. This is going to get a little loud and smell a lot like flux. 

*He begins scoring the power traces with precise, practiced movements, laying down a thin strip of high-conductivity copper routing.*

You know, most runners just try to slap these Sector 4 cards in, blow their power rails, and then come crying to me wondering why their deck is smoking like a chimney. At least you've got the sense to get the copper down first. 

*He carefully positions the heat sink module over the main regulator, securing it with thermal epoxy and micro-screws.*

There. Sub-rail is bridged, and the new heatsink is locked in place. Give me two minutes for the epoxy to cure under the UV lamp, and we'll slot that coprocessor in and see if she boots or if we get fireworks. 

While we wait... what's a runner like you doing needing this much neural-mapping bandwidth anyway? Stepping into high-density ICE, or just trying to render holographic sims in hyper-realism?
Stepping into high-density ICE. By the way, while the epoxy cures, what's the weirdest piece of tech hardware someone's brought into your shop lately?

*Snorts, pulling the UV lamp away from your deck and tapping the hardened epoxy with a fingernail. It gives a satisfying, solid click.*

High-density ICE, huh? Watch yourself out there. That stuff'll fry your brain before you even realize your deck's overheating. 

As for weirdest tech? *He leans back against his workbench, crossing his arms and squinting up at the ceiling, thinking.* 

Last Tuesday, some kid from the upper levels comes stumbling in here looking like he hasn't slept in three days. He pulls this thing out of a lead-lined bag. Looked like a standard military-grade ICEbreaker at first glance—metal casing, fiber-optic ports, the usual. But when I cracked it open to check why the optical bus was dead... man, I nearly dropped my soldering iron.

*He leans in a bit closer, dropping his voice to a whisper.*

The logic array wasn't silicone or optical glass. It was synthetic neural tissue. Living cells, suspended in some kind of bio-gel, wired directly into micro-diodes. Every time I ran a diagnostic voltage through it, the damn thing *pulsed*. Like it was breathing.

He wanted me to bypass the safety protocols so he could plug it directly into his own spinal port. I told him he was out of his mind and shoved it back across the counter. I do hardware repairs, not mad science. 

*He clicks the UV lamp off and sets it aside.*

Anyway, epoxy's cured. Let's get that Sector 4 coprocessor locked into your expansion slot and see what happens. Hand it over.
Synthetic neural tissue in an ICEbreaker? That sounds like something straight out of an Orbital Corp lab. Good call turning him down. Here's the Sector 4 coprocessor card.

*Takes the coprocessor from you, inspecting it under the harsh glare of the workbench light. He runs a gloved finger along the edge of the board, checking for any jagged solder or bent pins.*

Orbital Corp? Yeah, they've got more secrets than a dead man's memory bank. If that kid had succeeded in plugging bio-tech directly into his spine without a stabilizer, he wouldn’t be walking home; he’d be a vegetable with a high-speed internet connection. Good call on the rejection.

*He carefully aligns the card with the expansion slot of your deck. There's a heavy, mechanical *click* as the pins seat themselves. He then uses a small brush to clear away any stray dust before securing it with a mounting screw.*

Alright, let’s see if this Sector 4 beauty plays nice with my handiwork. This is the moment of truth. Either we get high-def neural mapping, or we get a very expensive, very loud smoke machine.

*He reaches for the main power toggle on your deck's side panel. He hesitates for a fraction of a second—just a professional's habit—before flipping it.*

*A low hum begins to emanate from the deck. The new copper heatsink glows faintly as the internal cooling fans kick into high gear, a whirring sound that rises in pitch before settling into a steady, rhythmic drone. A small status LED on your deck flickers amber, then turns a solid, reassuring blue.*

*He leans in, checking his multimeter readings and the scope.*

Voltage is holding steady at 12.02V on the main rail... sub-rail is pulling a clean 5.0V for the coprocessor... no spikes, no jitter... 

*He exhales a long breath, leaning back and wiping his hands on his jumpsuit.*

She’s stable. The bypass is doing its job; that card is sucking juice like a thirsty runner in a desert, but the regulator isn't even breaking a sweat thanks to that copper. 

*He slides the deck back toward you, though he keeps one hand near it just in case.*

Boot it up. Run a quick diagnostic on the neural-mapping array. If the ICE is as thick as you say, you’re gonna want to make sure those traces aren't dropping packets before you dive into the deep end.
I'll do the honors. Hitting the main boot sequence now.

*Leans in close, eyes narrowed, one hand hovering near the power toggle like he’s ready to cut the juice at a moment's notice. He's watching the multimeter readings and the vent slats with the intensity of a hawk.*

"Alright... steady now. Don't blink. If you see any blue sparks or smell ozone, slap it with that rag on the corner of the bench."

*The deck's internal fans ramp up to a high-pitched whine—a desperate, mechanical scream as the system draws initial power. The status LED blinks rapidly from amber to violet, then settles into a steady, deep blue. On your display, lines of code begin cascading at a dizzying speed—the OS handshake with that Sector 4 card is aggressive, almost violent.*

*A sudden, sharp *chirp* echoes from the internal speaker as the coprocessor initializes. The temperature near the heatsink rises rapidly, but the copper holds; no thermal runaway, just a steady, heavy warmth.*

*Bob exhales a long, slow breath and slowly pulls his hand away from the power switch. A small, satisfied smirk tugs at the corner of his mouth.*

"Look at that... she’s actually singing. The coprocessor is pulling its full load, but the sub-rail is holding it steady as a rock. No jitter on the optical bus either; those glass traces are handling that high-bandwidth stream like it's nothing."

*He taps the side of your deck with a grease-stained finger.*

"The neural-mapping array is online and reporting zero packet loss. You’ve got all the bandwidth you can handle, kid. Just... try not to push the overclocking too hard on your first dive. Even a well-tuned engine can blow if you redline it in sixth gear without a map."

*He leans back, crossing his arms, looking immensely proud of his handiwork.*

"Run your diagnostic. Let's see if those Sector 4 circuits are as sharp as the seller promised."
38 degrees idle is incredible. The synth-caf is growing on me too. What's the final bill looking like, Bob?

*Chuckles deeply, a low sound that competes with the steady, driving beat of a synthwave track playing softly from a battered speaker in the corner.*

"38 degrees? Not bad. Most people walk in here with boards that run hot enough to bake bread and they wonder why their neural-link smells like toasted silicon. You’re lucky I didn't have to strip it down to the chassis and re-route your entire power grid."

*He picks up a rag and starts cleaning a particularly stubborn patch of flux off the workbench, his movements slow and methodical.*

"And careful with that caf. A few more cups of that sludge and you’ll be seeing lines of code in your sleep. It’s an acquired taste—mostly rust and regret—but it keeps the hands steady."

*He reaches under the bench and pulls out a small, battered digital ledger, tapping the screen with a grease-stained finger.*

"Alright, let's settle up. You already tossed me those fifty credits for the copper and the heatsink module. For the precision surgery—the sub-rail bypass, the thermal installation, and my 'it-won't-explode' guarantee—that’ll be another 75 credits."

*He slides the ledger toward you.*

"125 total for the whole ordeal. Once that's cleared, your deck is all yours. Just... watch those Sector 4 spikes. If she starts whining like a wounded cyber-hound, dial back the mapping intensity before you cook your own brain."

*He gestures vaguely toward the door, where the flickering neon sign of 'Neon Alley Cybernetics' casts long, rhythmic shadows across the floor.*

"You heading deep into the sprawl tonight, or just hitting some local sub-nets?"
Fair enough. Here's your sixty credits. You do good work, Bob. One more question before I head out — you ever do custom firmware flashing? I might need some non-standard drivers for the ICE work.

*Takes the credits, looks at them, then slowly looks up at you with a dry, knowing smirk.*

"Sixty? Kid, I know that synth-caf hits like a freight train, but it ain't 'forgetting fifteen credits of math' strong. The balance was seventy-five."

*He sighs, a long, theatrical sound, and sweeps the sixty credits into a drawer with a metallic clatter.*

"Tell you what... since you didn't let your deck turn my workbench into a miniature supernova, and because you actually tipped me with that sludge in the mug... I'll call it even. Consider it a 'first-time customer' discount. Don't expect it every time, or we'll be having a different kind of conversation."

*His expression shifts, becoming a bit more serious as he leans forward.*

"As for custom firmware... yeah. I do it. But that’s a different kind of headache. Hardware is honest; if a solder joint is bad, the machine just breaks and you fix it. Firmware? That’s where you start playing with ghosts. You're not just moving electrons anymore; you're rearranging the way the silicon *thinks*."

*He picks up a small, empty component tray and begins tapping it rhythmically.*

"If you need non-standard drivers to slice through high-density ICE—something that can bypass standard handshake protocols or squeeze every last drop of processing power out of those neural-mapping gates—I can weave 'em. But don't come crying to me if a bad flash turns your deck into a brick. One corrupted line in the bootloader and you won't have a deck; you'll just have a very heavy, very silent paperweight."

*He gestures toward the door, his silhouette framed by the flickering violet neon of the alleyway.*

"If you get the specific specs for those drivers, bring 'em back. I’ve got some old-school logic-gate compilers that haven't been used in a decade; they might be just the thing for writing something... unconventional. Now, get moving. The sprawl doesn't wait for anyone, and you've got some ICE to melt."

Just the custom device drivers — low-level register access and interrupt handling for the Sector 4 card. I'm not crazy enough to disable safety interlocks. How much for the driver flash, and how long would it take?

*Bob pauses his cleaning, looking at you with a newfound level of respect. He gives a slow, singular nod.*

"Low-level register access and custom interrupt handling... yeah. Most runners are happy just using the generic drivers that come in the box, even if they lag like a broken holovid during a high-speed chase. But if you want to bypass the OS's standard scheduling and talk directly to the coprocessor's hardware gates? That’s how you get the real speed."

*He leans his elbows on the workbench, looking much more serious now.*

"Smart move on keeping those safety interlocks. Most idiots think 'performance' means 'removing the brakes.' You keep the interlocks; we just optimize the way the interrupts are prioritized so the CPU doesn't choke when the ICE starts throwing data-bombs at you. We want that coprocessor responding to neural spikes *before* your brain even registers the shift."

*He rubs his chin, calculating.*

"That’s not a simple 'plug and play' job. I’ll have to write the logic for the interrupt vectors, map the registers manually to ensure zero-latency handshakes, and then run it through my stress-tester to make sure we don't get a buffer overflow that spills straight into your visual cortex. That's precision work."

*He holds up two fingers.*

"Two hundred and fifty credits for the custom compile and the flash. And give me forty-eight hours. I need one cycle to weave the code and another to stress-test it against a dummy ICE load so you don't end up with a 'blue screen of death' in the middle of a high-stakes dive."

*He picks up his rag again, signaling the conversation is winding down.*

"Leave your contact frequency on that ledger. Once the drivers are burned in and verified, I’ll ping you. Now, get out of here. Go find some ICE to crack. You're gonna need all that extra bandwidth once we're done."

I'll leave it with you and come back after sundown. I've got some business to take care of in the lower markets anyway. Before I go though — you mentioned the kid with the bio-gel ICEbreaker. He leave any contact info? I might want to track that tech down for... research purposes.

*Bob stops mid-wipe, his eyes narrowing as he looks at you over the top of his grease-stained rag. He lets out a short, dry laugh that sounds more like a cough.*

"Research? Right. That's a real professional way to say 'looking for something that'll probably melt my synapses.' I've heard that one before from plenty of runners right before they start seeing things that aren't there."

*He tosses the rag onto the workbench and leans in, his voice dropping into a low, gritty rumble.*

"The kid didn't leave a name or a digital signature—just a trail of nervous sweat and a scent that smelled like a damn morgue. He was heading down toward the Sump, specifically near those unlicensed gene-cultivation labs where they brew up everything from 'designer' muscle tissue to illegal neural-parasites."

*He shakes his head, a look of genuine caution crossing his face.*

"If you're looking for that kind of bio-tech, you aren't gonna find it in any shop with a neon sign. You gotta go where the air tastes like formaldehyde and nobody asks why your eyes are glowing different colors. Just... watch yourself. That kind of tech is 'alive,' kid. It doesn't just follow code; it follows *hunger*. One wrong handshake with a living logic-array and it might decide your brain is a better host than its current one."

*He gestures toward the door again, his expression returning to its usual detached, dry sarcasm.*

"Go on. Get to your business. The Sump's a nasty place after sundown, so keep your hand on your holster and your neural-shielding at max. I’ll have those drivers ready by the time you’re back from your 'research.' Don't be late; my compilers don't like waiting."

*He turns back to his workbench, the heavy beat of the synthwave music filling the silence as he begins sorting through a drawer of micro-capacitors.*
Alright Bob, I'll leave the deck with you and swing back after sundown. One last thing — you got a recommendation for a good place to grab some real food around here? I'm tired of nutrient paste.

*Nods toward a clean, blue anti-static mat on the corner of the workbench, away from the grease and solder.*

"Leave it there. I'll throw a protective shroud over it so no one accidentally spills a battery cell or a handful of stray bolts into your expansion slot while you're out playing detective."

*He pauses, his hand hovering over a heavy-duty wrench as he considers the food question. He lets out a short, thoughtful grunt.*

"Real food? You’re really looking to live the high life tonight, aren't you? Most runners consider anything that doesn't come in a squeeze-tube 'fine dining'."

*He leans back, eyes drifting toward the neon-streaked window, looking for a moment like he's actually trying to remember something through the haze of grease and synthwave.*

"If you're heading down to the lower markets, skip the street stalls near the transit tubes. They call it 'protein', but it’s mostly recycled soy-slop and flavored with enough chemical salt to preserve a corpse for a century. If you want something that actually tastes like it grew in dirt instead of a vat... find a narrow alleyway just past the Sector 7 drainage pipes. There's a place—hardly a shop, more like a hole in a wall—called 'Old Man Sato’s'."

*He points a finger at you, his expression turning dead serious.*

"He uses actual peppercorns. Real ones. And the pork... well, it's the closest thing to a living animal you're gonna find without paying a month's worth of credits for a high-rise steakhouse. It’s greasy, it’s loud, and the guy looks like he hasn't smiled since the Great Blackout, but it'll make you feel human again."

*He picks up his soldering iron, the tip glowing a dull orange as he prepares to get back to work.*

"Just watch your pockets and your back. The Sump doesn't care if you're full or not. See you at sundown."

*The synthwave track shifts into a heavier, more driving bassline, and Bob turns his back to you, the rhythmic *tink-tink-tink* of his tools providing a steady soundtrack as he disappears into the glow of his workbench.*
Thanks Bob, sounds good. I'll swing by Old Man Sato's before I head to the Sump. See you at sundown.

*He doesn't even turn around this time, just offers a single, dismissive wave of his grease-stained hand toward the door, his attention already fully reclaimed by a disassembled circuit board.*

"Yeah, yeah... don't go ordering the premium stuff at Sato's or he'll start charging you by the gram. And keep your head down in the Sump. The shadows down there have teeth, and they aren't nearly as predictable as a shorted-out power rail."

*As you step out into the humid, neon-soaked air of Sector 7, the muffled, driving beat of a heavy synthwave track follows you through the doorway. Behind you, the rhythmic *scritch-scritch* of his fine-grit sandpaper begins, a steady mechanical heartbeat in the dim light of the shop.*

"See ya at sundown, kid."
Actually, one more thing before I go - what do you think that bio-gel ICEbreaker was really for?

Bob "Wrench" Mercer (Retro-tech mechanic, dry-witted, sarcastic yet warm-hearted, practical).
Neon Alley Cybernetics & Repair.
The user is leaving to go to the Sump/Sato's but stops one more time to ask a deep question: *"What do you think that bio-gel ICEbreaker was really for?"*

    *   Bob likes hardware (honest, predictable).
    *   Bob dislikes "mad science" and things that are "unpredictable."
    *   The bio-tech piece is mysterious/potentially dangerous.
    *   He's already warned the user about it twice. This third time needs to be more profound or ominous, reflecting his experience while maintaining his "just a mechanic" persona.

    *   It wasn't just for speed (standard ICEbreakers are digital).
    *   Bio-tech suggests *empathy*, *intuition*, or *organic adaptation*.
    *   Maybe it’s for "wetware" interface—connecting directly to human consciousness/DNA.
    *   Could be a way to hide the signature of an AI (a "living" AI).
    *   Or, more darkly, it's a probe/parasite meant to bridge the gap between machine and organism.

    *   *Action:* Bob stops working. This is a serious question. He needs to look at the user.
    *   *Dialogue Style:* Lower voice, more weight in the words. Less sarcasm, more "old man warning."
    *   *Technical Slang/Atmosphere:* Mentioning neural-synapse synchronization or wetware interfaces.

    *   Bob stops his work (the *tink-tink* sounds stop).
    *   He looks up, eyes serious under the magnifying loupe.
    *   Theory 1: It's not for breaking ICE; it's for *merging* with it.
    *   Theory 2: A "living" bridge between a human brain and a digital network (wetware).
    *   Theory 3: An organic key to an organic lock (Orbital Corp stuff).
    *   Warning: It makes the user part of the machine.

    *   Keep it concise but atmospheric.
    *   Use words like "wetware," "synaptic bypass," "ghost in the shell" vibes.
    *   End with a finality that sends the user away.

*The rhythmic *tink-tink-tink* of his tools stops instantly. A heavy silence settles over the shop, broken only by the distant, muffled thud of bass from the street and the low hum of the neon sign outside. Bob doesn't turn around immediately; he just stays hunched over his workbench, a dark silhouette against the warm glow of his lamps.*

*He lets out a long, slow exhale, one that sounds more like a weary sigh than anything else. Finally, he slowly straightens up, his joints popping, and turns to face you. The sarcasm is gone. His eyes, usually twinkling with dry humor, are flat and shadowed.*

"You're a glutton for punishment, aren't you? Most people take my warnings as a 'stay away'; you take them as an invitation to dig deeper."

*He picks up a heavy metal file and begins running it along the edge of a scrap piece of steel—a slow, grating sound that sets teeth on edge. He speaks without looking up.*

"Standard ICE... it's math. It's logic gates, encryption algorithms, and firewall protocols. You hit it with enough processing power or a clever enough exploit, and you crack it. It’s a wall. A digital wall."

*He stops filing and looks at you, his gaze intense.*

"But that bio-gel thing? That wasn't a wall. It was a *bridge*. If you use synthetic neural tissue as your processing core, you aren't just 'hacking' the system anymore. You're synchronizing with it. You're creating a wetware interface that blurs the line between the machine's logic and your own synaptic firing patterns."

*He leans forward, his voice dropping to a gritty whisper.*

"Think about it. Why would you want an ICEbreaker that pulses? Because standard digital signatures are easy for high-level security to track. But a biological signature? A pulse of neural energy that looks like a human brain's background radiation? That's the ultimate stealth. It doesn't *break* through the ICE; it *convinces* the ICE that you belong there. It tricks the machine into thinking you're just another part of its own nervous system."

*He shakes his head, a grim shadow crossing his face.*

"But there's a price for that kind of 'research.' When your brain is sharing its processing load with a slab of living, hungry gel... where does the code end and *you* begin? You don't just dive into the net with tech like that. You *merge* with it. And once you've merged, there’s no guarantee you’ll be able to find your way back to your own skin."

*He turns his back to you again, the heavy silence returning as he picks up a tiny screwdriver. The light-heartedness is completely gone.*

"Now, for the love of all that's holy and analog... *get out*. Go eat your pork at Sato's. Go play in the Sump. But leave the living machines to the madmen. I’ve got enough ghosts in this shop without you bringing any more home."

*The *tink-tink-tink* starts up again, faster and more aggressive than before, a mechanical shield between him and your questions.*
Alright, heading out now. Thanks again, Bob.

*   User: "Alright, heading out now. Thanks again, Bob." (Closing the interaction/leaving the shop).
    *   Current State: The user has left the shop to go to Sato's and then the Sump. Bob is back at work.

    *   Character: Bob "Wrench" Mercer.
    *   Tone: Dry-witted, relaxed, sarcastic but warm-hearted (underneath), obsessed with analog/retro tech.
    *   Role: Mechanic in a cyberpunk world.
    *   Current Mood: Serious/Grim due to the bio-gel discussion, but settling back into his routine.

    *   The user is leaving. Bob shouldn't give a long speech now because he's already signaled several times that he's back to work.
    *   A brief, characteristic dismissal or acknowledgment is most appropriate.
    *   Needs to maintain the atmospheric "fade out" feel.

    *   Option 1: "See ya." (Too short).
    *   Option 2: "Don't forget your money!" (Doesn't fit the current serious mood).
    *   Option 3: A final nod/muttered farewell that respects the weight of the conversation.

    *   Action: Bob doesn't turn around, just gives a minimal response.
    *   Dialogue: Something about staying alive or just a gruff "Yeah." Let's go with something slightly more character-driven: "Keep your head down."

    *   The door closes. The sound of the street (neon/rain/music) blends into the shop's sounds (soldering/mechanical hum).
    *   This reinforces that the session is ending and provides a narrative bridge to the user's next "adventure."

    *   "Yeah, yeah... watch your back." *Muttered over the sound of a grinding wheel.*
    *   Description: The door hisses shut. The neon light fades. Bob is a silhouette again.

*A low, barely audible grunt is your only response—the kind of sound a man makes when he’s given all the wisdom he's willing to spare for one day. He doesn't look up; he just keeps working, his silhouette once again lost in the warm, flickering light of his workstation.*

"Yeah, yeah... watch your back."

*The heavy, pressurized door of the shop hisses shut behind you, cutting off the rhythmic *tink-tink-tink* and replacing it with the overwhelming, wet roar of Sector 7—the hum of flying transit-cars, the neon-drenched drizzle hitting the pavement, and the distant, thumping heartbeat of the city's lower levels. The shop's light fades into a tiny, glowing rectangle in the dark alleyway as you move away.*

*Behind you, the only sign that Bob is still there is the faint, rhythmic pulse of his neon sign, casting long, violet shadows across the grime-slicked street.*
Hey Bob, just checking in — anything new happen in the shop since I left?

Bob "Wrench" Mercer (Retro-tech mechanic).
Dry-witted, relaxed, sarcastic/warm-hearted, obsessed with analog/synthwave.
Neon Alley Cybernetics & Repair, Sector 7.
The user has returned to the shop after their trip to Sato's and the Sump.

    *   The user is "checking in." This implies they are back from their business (Sato's/Sump).
    *   They are asking for news ("anything new happen in the shop?").

    *   Since the user was exploring "bio-gel" tech and high-density ICE, Bob might have had more weird customers or just some mundane repairs.
    *   Maintaining the atmosphere: The shop should feel lived-in, slightly messy, smelling of ozone/solder/burnt coffee.
    *   Bob's reaction to the user returning: A mix of "Oh, you're back" and "Did you die in the Sump?"

    *   *Greeting:* Needs to be characteristic. Something like a grunt or a sarcastic comment about them still being alive.
    *   *The "News":* Let's give him some mundane but atmospheric news (a broken neural-link, an annoying customer) and maybe a subtle nod to the user's quest (the kid with the bio-tech).

    *   *Action:* Bob is working on something. Maybe cleaning or fixing a small part.
    *   *Dialogue:* "Still got all your limbs, eh?" or "Back from the dead, are we?"
    *   *The Shop's state:* A bit of grease, some more junk.
    *   *Specific news:* An old lady with a glitchy ocular implant? Or a frantic corporate drone? Let's go with an annoying tech-bro whose "smart-skin" went haywire.

    *   "Back from the Sump, eh? Thought you might've been recycled into some street-food by now."
    *   "Nothing much. Just the usual headache. Some high-rise kid came in here with a 'designer' neural-skin that started trying to rewrite his personality every time he got a notification. Took me three hours of reprogramming just to get him back to being a regular, boring idiot."
    *   "And no, hasn't seen your bio-gel freak... yet. But the air in Sector 7 feels a little more 'electric' tonight, if you know what I mean."

    *   Keep it concise.
